To stop this kind of phish (which is a failure of the human element, not the technology or the method of security) never click urls sent via txt and if you have to, use a separate browser on your mobile device than the one set as default. This stop people getting at your auto-logged in accounts as well as any cookie/session related hacks.

If you are on mobile, there is no reason to use any google product outside of the provided apps, so as a matter of procedure, you should not change your password from your mobile device, but wait until you can get to your desktop.

Once on your desktop, test any password reset request url in a safe browser, using extensions like uMatrix and uBlock.
Always check the address in the URL bar as often they are hiding in what looks like a legit url.

A safe browser is one you never use to access apple/facebook/google/twitter etc as a daily thing, it is one set specifically for unsafe web activities (porn lol) where you would expect redirect, or click over/under hacks etc.

An easy example is to use one browser for your banking, email, social media etc and use voat in a different browser.
In firefox this is easy to set up by using different profiles and launching them with -P "$profileName" --NO-REMOTE in a windows shortcut or shell.

Another fast way to achieve this is to use 'portable apps' versions, which all have separate storage sections and make it easier to have multiple accounts without installing any extra software.

The other thing to note specific to google, is the message they send about possible unauthorized access is sent via email to you fall back email accounts as well, which includes the location of the suspected hack.
If you don't have these and all you got was a text message, it's pretty obvious it's a phish attempt and you should make sure everything is good by going to a 'secure' computer and browser and changing your password anyway.
